prompt: What does `latest` mean when reading a secret?

choices.text: Every version, joined
choices.why: A read returns one version.

choices.text: The newest enabled version
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Version 1, the original
choices.why: That is the oldest.

choices.text: The version created most recently, enabled or not
choices.why: A disabled version is skipped.

prompt: Why is the accessor role granted on the secret rather than on the project?
hint: What else is in the project?

choices.text: It would reach all the other secrets too
choices.why: Right. Including the ones that are not its business.

choices.text: It is cheaper per access
choices.why: Access price does not depend on where the role is.

choices.text: Rotation requires it
choices.why: Rotation is about the topic, not the role.

choices.text: Project-level grants are not allowed for secrets
choices.why: They are allowed, and too broad.

prompt: A version is disabled. What can still be done with it?

choices.text: Move it to another secret
choices.why: Versions do not move between secrets.

choices.text: Read it, with a warning
choices.why: Disabled versions cannot be read.

choices.text: Bring it back in seconds
choices.why: Right. Which is why disable comes before destroy.

choices.text: Nothing: it is gone
choices.why: That is destroyed, not disabled.

prompt: An account makes 110,000 secret accesses in a month. At 0.03 USD per 10,000 after the first 10,000, what do they cost?
Why does readsecret.py print the length and two characters rather than the value?
hint: Where does standard output go on Cloud Run?

choices.text: Python cannot print the whole file
choices.why: It can; it should not.

choices.text: The value is encrypted and unreadable
choices.why: The file holds the plain value.

choices.text: Printed text ends up in logs
choices.why: Right. A logged password is readable by every log viewer.

choices.text: Printing it would rotate it
choices.why: Printing does not rotate anything.

prompt: A rotation job adds a new version. Which instances use it without a restart?

choices.text: Those rereading a mounted latest file
choices.why: Right. And whose code rereads the file on a failed connection.

choices.text: Those reading it from an environment variable
choices.why: Variables are resolved once, at start.

choices.text: None: every new version needs a redeploy
choices.why: A mounted latest file does not.

choices.text: All of them, at once
choices.why: Variables do not change in a running instance.

prompt: What does `sensitive = true` on a Terraform variable do?

choices.text: Hides it in the terminal
choices.why: Right. The state still holds it in plain text.

choices.text: Stores it in Secret Manager
choices.why: Terraform does nothing of the kind on its own.

choices.text: Keeps it out of the state
choices.why: It is in the state, as the lesson showed.

choices.text: Encrypts it in the state
choices.why: grep found it three times in the state.

prompt: Why does the shop's Terraform create the secret but no secret version?
hint: Where would the value end up?

choices.text: Its value would sit in the state
choices.why: Right. The state would become a second copy of every secret.

choices.text: The provider has no resource for versions
choices.why: It has one; using it puts the value in the state.

choices.text: Versions must be created by Google
choices.why: Anyone with the permission adds versions.

choices.text: Terraform cannot read standard input
choices.why: That is not the reason.

prompt: `terraform plan` shows `(sensitive value)` for a password. Somebody concludes the state bucket needs no special protection. What is wrong?
hint: Hidden on screen is not hidden in the file.

choices.text: Nothing: sensitive values are never stored
choices.why: They are stored, in plain text.

choices.text: It sits in the state in plain text
choices.why: Right. Whoever reads the state reads it.

choices.text: The value is only stored for one hour
choices.why: It stays as long as the state does.

choices.text: Only that the plan file needs protection
choices.why: The state needs it as much.

prompt: Put the database-password rotation in an order that breaks nothing.
items: Create the new password in the database
Add it as a new version
Wait until every instance has picked it up
Revoke the old password and disable its version
trap: Revoking first is the slip: every running instance breaks at once.

prompt: When `next_rotation_time` arrives, what does Secret Manager do?

choices.text: Publishes SECRET_ROTATE to the topic
choices.why: Right. Something subscribed does the work.

choices.text: Generates a new password and adds it
choices.why: It changes nothing itself.

choices.text: Disables the current version
choices.why: That would break the service.

choices.text: Changes the password in the database
choices.why: It knows nothing about the database.

prompt: A password is found in a public repository. Which steps follow? Choose all that apply.
hint: Treat it as known to everybody.

choices.text: Add a new version
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Revoke the old password in the database
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Delete the commit and consider it handled
choices.why: No. History and forks keep copies.

choices.text: Disable the old version
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Wait to see whether anybody uses it
choices.why: No. By then the damage is done.

prompt: The role that lets a service account read a secret's versions is `roles/secretmanager.___`.
Who read the database password last month? Where is the answer?

choices.text: Nowhere: reads are not recorded
choices.why: They are, once data-access logging is on.

choices.text: In the Terraform state
choices.why: The state knows nothing about reads.

choices.text: In the secret's version list
choices.why: Versions record values, not readers.

choices.text: In data-access audit logs, if they were on
choices.why: Right. Which account, which version, when.
